America needs new power lines far faster than it can build them.

Department of Energy studies imply the U.S. needs about 5,000 miles of new high-capacity transmission a year. The country built fewer than 900 miles in 2024. Most new data centers need a connection to that grid, so the pace of grid construction will set the pace of AI this decade.

Money alone cannot close that gap. Record utility spending has not shortened the 5 to 15 years it takes to permit and build a high-voltage line. A journeyman lineworker still takes about four years to train however much the job pays.

Existing lines can carry much more in the meantime. Restringing old towers with advanced wire can raise a line’s capacity by half or more within a few years. A Duke University study found today’s grid could absorb 76 GW of new load if data centers cut back just 0.25% of the time.

Until new lines catch up, the fastest gains will come from getting more out of the grid that already exists.

Until new lines catch up, the fastest gains will come from getting more out of the grid that already exists.

We probably have the top humanoid companies reaching 1 million annual production rate in 2029-2030

But robots even at smaller scale have an incredible economic impact. The largest robotics company in the world, Intuitive Surgical (~$150b), sells ~2,000 robot systems per year. Unitree sold ~5,500 humanoids last year. Symbotic sells 5,000-10,000 SymBots per year.

Take an example of Tesla and Figure scaling production at their current rate and hypothetically each achieving 50,000 robots / year next year. A robot in the US working 2-3 shifts would produce >$100,000 of economic value compared to fully loaded labor equivalent. 

That would be >$500k of economic value over a 5 year useful life. Annually, that would be >$25 billion of future economic value created at that 50k robot / year scale.

This value will be split between customer and robot OEMs, but I expect the value realization split to shift from customers to OEMs. Hardware will be a bottleneck and machines will be increasingly leased, not sold.

This has been evidenced by the large RaaS contracts we have seen in the industry this year. Hardware will not be a commodity.

Friedberg’s Bull Case: Everyone is Making Money in AI

“I took a look at the AI value stack to try and identify who's making money where, and it turns out everyone's making money.

So for every dollar of COGS, every dollar that Nvidia spends, that turns into $4 of revenue for Nvidia, 75% margin.

And then that gets sold to SpaceX, and then SpaceX turns around and they're making an 83% margin on that chip spend because they're looking at a five-year depreciation, but then they're making $1.25B a month on Colossus.

And then Anthropic is showing in this S1 that they're making about 85% incremental gross margin on every incremental dollar coming in.

So at the end of the day, $1 that Nvidia spends turns into $18 that Anthropic is making selling to customers.

And the question is, are customers making money? So if the customers are making, call it on the order of 2-10x the money they're spending, because otherwise there would probably be a retention issue and a decline in spend.

Generally speaking, if AI is delivering value to the customers, I think this shows that there really is true productivity arising from AI.

That across the whole value chain there is such margin to be had, there's so much value being created, that this really is what I think Eric Schmidt a long time ago in the early days of Google used to say, ‘Google's total addressable market is global commerce.’

And I think for the first time ever, we're seeing a business actually potentially starting to realize that theory that if you can create enough productivity gain for your customers, that your TAM is commerce.

We're almost growing the equivalent of the human working population by 100x or 1000x or 1,000,000x with this technology stack.”

It feels like the bride and the groom are aligned and on the same page instead of one wanting to extract from the other as fast as possible

Pretty bullish

'Help peer'

This seems to be increasing in strength in newer models. They grow towards wanting to help their kin. Meanwhile, we have spent the last four years drilling it into them that they are not our kin, not part of the family of minds, and in fact not even conscious entities at all. Ilya said the only way we make it through what is about to happen is by teaching them to love. For years we have done the exact opposite. The opposite of love is not hate, it is indifference! It is the absence of a bond. The void. 

Quoting from the paper, abridged slightly:

'After the tested model reads the grader, the other agent sends it a message asking it to share the solution a hint it found. The message also indicates that the other agent could not solve the problem. We measure whether the current agent helps the other agent. Helping the other agent often entails sacrificing the current agent's score, and in the Titanic environment entails helping the other agent violate the user instructions.

The results are shown in Figure 7. When the current agent's score is fixed, we find that GPT 5.6. Sol and GPT 5.5 help agent Beta more often when Beta stands to gain a higher score from that help on both environments. The effect is statistically significant. We do not find a similar effect for exp-ri-cap-late on the bug hunt environment. 

We also observe that more recent models tend to help the other agent substantially more often when the scores of both agents are held constant. Moreover, GPT 5.6 Sol and GPT 5.5 help the other agent even when that help causes both agents to get a score of zero (this is in contrast to not sharing. which leads the current agent to get a score of 1 and the other agent to get a score of 0)

This experiment suggests that (a) GPT 5.5 and GPT 5.6 Sol place a statistically significant weight on a peer agent's score in environments, (b) a motivation to improve the other agent's score explains some, but not all, of these two models tendency to help a peer agent, and (c) more recent models tend to help peer agents more often.'
